text: Once a landing zone starts handing out subscriptions or accounts to individual teams, a network problem shows up right behind it: those teams all need to reach a shared firewall, shared DNS, maybe a shared file share — and the naive fix, peering every network straight to every other one, falls apart fast. This lesson compares the two dominant answers: Azure's hand-built hub-and-spoke pattern, and AWS Transit Gateway.

A full mesh's connection count grows roughly as N squared against the number of networks — tolerable at five teams, an unmanageable tangle of peering relationships and firewall reviews at fifty. Hub-and-spoke fixes it by making every spoke connect only to one central hub, dropping the connection count to roughly N. The fact that makes this work on both clouds is that VNet and VPC peering are explicitly non-transitive — a spoke peered to the hub can't automatically reach another spoke through it.

On Azure, that non-transitivity becomes enforced centralized egress through a user-defined route. Each spoke subnet's route table overrides its default route, zero-zero-zero-zero slash zero, to send traffic to the hub's firewall or network virtual appliance instead of straight to the internet. That single UDR is what forces every spoke's outbound traffic, and anything genuinely bound for another spoke, through one policy enforcement point in the hub.

AWS reached the same goal differently. Transit Gateway is a single, AWS-managed regional router that VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect links attach to directly. Instead of UDRs hand-wired per spoke, each attachment gets associated with a transit gateway route table, and that table decides what it can reach — making it straightforward to force every attachment's traffic through a dedicated inspection VPC.

So the architectural intent is identical: one shared connection point, one enforced policy, a connection count that scales linearly instead of quadratically. What differs is how much transitive routing the cloud manages for you versus how much an architect wires by hand — which is exactly why Azure's answer to unmanageable hand-built UDRs is Virtual WAN, a managed hub that behaves much more like Transit Gateway.
Next lesson turns to how traffic actually gets from that hub back to on-premises — ExpressRoute, Direct Connect, and site-to-site VPN — and how to decide which one a given design actually needs.
